analysis.one_liner: Orders the EPA to set water pollution limits for PFAS "forever chemicals" discharged by industry.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or vote; no roll call ever occurred.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made "forever chemicals" used in nonstick cookware, weatherproof clothing, and industrial processes, and they may have adverse human health effects. The bill would require the EPA to review industrial sources that discharge PFAS into water, then set legally binding limits on that discharge (effluent limitations and pretreatment standards) and publish water quality criteria. It set deadlines: water quality criteria for covered substances within 2 years, and final discharge limits for priority industries (organic chemicals/plastics, pulp and paper, and textile mills) within 4 years.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink tap water, eat fish, or live near industrial dischargers—essentially everyone exposed to PFAS through water. PFAS contamination of drinking water has been widely linked to health risks. Tighter discharge limits would reduce the amount of these chemicals entering waterways at the source, before they reach drinking water systems.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to set enforceable effluent limitations and pretreatment standards for PFAS discharged from industrial point sources, rather than leaving these chemicals essentially unregulated at the source.
Requires EPA to publish water quality criteria for PFAS within 2 years, giving states and water utilities a scientific benchmark for safe levels.
Targets priority industries—organic chemicals and plastics, pulp and paper, and textile mills—accounting for major industrial PFAS discharge pathways.

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge PFAS in their wastewater—chemical makers, plastics manufacturers, pulp and paper mills, and textile mills—would bear compliance costs to treat or eliminate PFAS from their discharge. These costs could be passed to consumers in product prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for industrial dischargers could be substantial, since effective PFAS treatment technology is still developing and expensive.
Tightening effluent limits alone does not clean up PFAS already in the environment; remediation of existing contamination would require separate, much larger efforts.
Setting strict limits on a still-evolving science could require repeated revisions as toxicity data improves, creating regulatory uncertainty for facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit of reducing PFAS entering waterways is broad and durable—PFAS do not break down and accumulate in people's bodies and the environment. The cost falls on a concentrated set of industrial facilities, which is the normal design of pollution regulation. The main honest caveat is that compliance technology for PFAS was immature, and the bill addresses new discharge rather than cleaning up existing contamination.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in December 2019 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote through the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Gillibrand with four Democratic cosponsors (Durbin, Merkley, Blumenthal, Markey) in December 2019.
Referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day; no further action was taken.
The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial dischargers of PFAS—chemical, plastics, pulp and paper, and textile facilities—avoided new federal discharge limits. The public gained nothing, as PFAS discharge remained unregulated at the source under this bill's approach.
